cards.explanation: It is associated with the outer membrane, unlike the protein exotoxins discussed in the other lecture.
cards.text: The classical Gram-negative bacterial endotoxin is {{c1::lipopolysaccharide (LPS)}}.
cards.question: The classical Gram-negative bacterial endotoxin is {{c1::lipopolysaccharide (LPS)}}.

cards.explanation: These and muramyl peptides can activate host responses, but their chemistry and recognition pathways are not identical to LPS.
cards.text: Gram-positive lipoteichoic acids are described in the lecture as {{c1::endotoxin-like}}, rather than true LPS endotoxin.
cards.question: Gram-positive lipoteichoic acids are described in the lecture as {{c1::endotoxin-like}}, rather than true LPS endotoxin.

cards.explanation: The source notes release from viable cells. LPS may also be shed in outer-membrane vesicles; the later claim that only cell-free LPS is active is too absolute.
cards.text: Living Gram-negative bacteria can release LPS without complete {{c1::cell lysis}}.
cards.question: Living Gram-negative bacteria can release LPS without complete {{c1::cell lysis}}.

cards.explanation: Complement-mediated membrane damage, phagocytic killing and some antibiotics are source examples. This does not mean indicated antibiotics should be withheld.
cards.text: Bacterial disintegration can increase the release of {{c1::endotoxin}}.
cards.question: Bacterial disintegration can increase the release of {{c1::endotoxin}}.

cards.explanation: The source illustrates interacting host systems, not a single isolated toxic reaction.
cards.text: Endotoxin can disturb inflammatory, complement and {{c1::coagulation}} cascades.
cards.question: Endotoxin can disturb inflammatory, complement and {{c1::coagulation}} cascades.

cards.explanation: The diagram distinguishes this from the inner membrane and the intervening peptidoglycan layer.
cards.text: LPS is located in the {{c1::outer membrane}} of the typical Gram-negative envelope.
cards.question: LPS is located in the {{c1::outer membrane}} of the typical Gram-negative envelope.

cards.explanation: Its structure strongly influences inflammatory recognition; the polysaccharide regions have distinct roles.
cards.text: The membrane-anchoring and principal toxic component of LPS is {{c1::lipid A}}.
cards.question: The membrane-anchoring and principal toxic component of LPS is {{c1::lipid A}}.

cards.explanation: It connects the membrane-associated lipid region with the repeating outer polysaccharide.
cards.text: The region between lipid A and the O-antigen is the {{c1::core oligosaccharide}}.
cards.question: The region between lipid A and the O-antigen is the {{c1::core oligosaccharide}}.

cards.explanation: Its antigenic differences contribute to serotyping; variability is not itself the sole determinant of endotoxin potency.
cards.text: The variable repeating outer polysaccharide is the {{c1::O-antigen}}.
cards.question: The variable repeating outer polysaccharide is the {{c1::O-antigen}}.

cards.explanation: The core also contains Kdo, which is an eight-carbon sugar rather than another heptose.
cards.text: The LPS core can contain seven-carbon sugars called {{c1::heptoses}}.
cards.question: The LPS core can contain seven-carbon sugars called {{c1::heptoses}}.

cards.explanation: It is not a heat-labile protein exotoxin. Heat stability does not mean no validated processing method can ever remove or inactivate endotoxin.
cards.text: LPS is relatively {{c1::heat stable}}.
cards.question: LPS is relatively {{c1::heat stable}}.

cards.explanation: This corrects the slide’s parenthetical seven-carbon description of ketodeoxyoctonate. The exact core composition varies by organism.
cards.text: Kdo in the LPS core is an {{c1::eight-carbon sugar}}.
cards.question: Kdo in the LPS core is an {{c1::eight-carbon sugar}}.

cards.explanation: The lipid A and short core remain; absence of the repeating O-chain does not mean absence of endotoxin.
cards.text: A truncated endotoxin lacking the long O-antigen repeat chain is called {{c1::lipooligosaccharide (LOS)}}.
cards.question: A truncated endotoxin lacking the long O-antigen repeat chain is called {{c1::lipooligosaccharide (LOS)}}.

cards.explanation: The source also names other genera, but their structures vary by species; do not make its genus list a universal rule for all Bordetella or Bacteroides.
cards.text: Neisseria provides a clinical example of an organism with {{c1::LOS}} rather than a long O-antigen-bearing LPS.
cards.question: Neisseria provides a clinical example of an organism with {{c1::LOS}} rather than a long O-antigen-bearing LPS.

cards.explanation: The source connects carbohydrate regions with physical presentation. Activity is context dependent, not determined only by the presence of O-antigen.
cards.text: The main toxic activity resides in lipid A, while polysaccharides affect properties such as {{c1::solubility and aggregation}}.
cards.question: The main toxic activity resides in lipid A, while polysaccharides affect properties such as {{c1::solubility and aggregation}}.

cards.explanation: The slide depicts several aggregate forms. Its smaller-micelle/greater-activity statement is not a universal size-only law of toxicity.
cards.text: Free amphipathic LPS can organise into aggregates such as {{c1::micelles}}.
cards.question: Free amphipathic LPS can organise into aggregates such as {{c1::micelles}}.

cards.explanation: LBP assists transfer of LPS to host recognition machinery.
cards.text: The blood protein initially binding LPS in the illustrated pathway is {{c1::LPS-binding protein (LBP)}}.
cards.question: The blood protein initially binding LPS in the illustrated pathway is {{c1::LPS-binding protein (LBP)}}.

cards.explanation: CD14 is not itself the full signalling receptor. Soluble CD14 can support responses of cells with little membrane CD14.
cards.text: The host co-receptor helping transfer LPS towards TLR4 is {{c1::CD14}}.
cards.question: The host co-receptor helping transfer LPS towards TLR4 is {{c1::CD14}}.

cards.explanation: The source emphasises TLR4; MD-2 is the associated LPS-binding co-receptor needed to interpret that simplified account.
cards.text: The principal receptor complex for canonical extracellular LPS signalling is {{c1::TLR4–MD-2}}.
cards.question: The principal receptor complex for canonical extracellular LPS signalling is {{c1::TLR4–MD-2}}.

cards.explanation: Its activation promotes expression of inflammatory mediators rather than making LPS itself a cytokine.
cards.text: The transcriptional pathway labelled downstream of LPS recognition is {{c1::NF-κB}}.
cards.question: The transcriptional pathway labelled downstream of LPS recognition is {{c1::NF-κB}}.

cards.explanation: These amplify host responses and contribute to systemic effects when activation is excessive.
cards.text: LPS-stimulated macrophages release {{c1::inflammatory cytokines}}.
cards.question: LPS-stimulated macrophages release {{c1::inflammatory cytokines}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts this with dysregulated systemic activation. No universal safe or toxic concentration is supplied.
cards.text: Limited LPS recognition can support protective {{c1::innate immune activation}}.
cards.question: Limited LPS recognition can support protective {{c1::innate immune activation}}.

cards.explanation: The source lists lung and kidney failure as possible severe effects; these are not inevitable consequences of any detectable LPS.
cards.text: Excessive systemic host activation can produce hypotension and {{c1::organ dysfunction}}.
cards.question: Excessive systemic host activation can produce hypotension and {{c1::organ dysfunction}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s “large amounts of LPS = sepsis” is shorthand, not a diagnostic definition. Sepsis can occur with pathogens that do not produce LPS.
cards.text: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated response to {{c1::infection}}.
cards.question: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated response to {{c1::infection}}.

cards.explanation: Vascular and inflammatory disturbances can impair perfusion. A single symptom does not establish sepsis or shock.
cards.text: Low blood pressure in severe endotoxin-associated illness is {{c1::hypotension}}.
cards.question: Low blood pressure in severe endotoxin-associated illness is {{c1::hypotension}}.

cards.explanation: The slide also lists increased respiratory rate. These findings are non-specific; severe infection does not always present with high fever.
cards.text: A systemic increase in heart rate is {{c1::tachycardia}}.
cards.question: A systemic increase in heart rate is {{c1::tachycardia}}.

cards.explanation: Invasive disease occurs in a subset of infections; carriage does not inevitably progress to meningitis.
cards.text: Neisseria meningitidis commonly colonises the {{c1::nasopharynx}}.
cards.question: Neisseria meningitidis commonly colonises the {{c1::nasopharynx}}.

cards.explanation: They can then reach meninges/CSF. Endotoxin-associated inflammation contributes to permeability changes, but crossing is not explained solely by one toxin.
cards.text: Invasive meningococci can reach the bloodstream and cross the {{c1::blood–brain barrier}}.
cards.question: Invasive meningococci can reach the bloodstream and cross the {{c1::blood–brain barrier}}.

cards.explanation: The source’s clinical photograph is covered; the deck preserves that cover and does not claim to diagnose hidden pathology.
cards.text: Meningococcal endotoxin can promote destructive {{c1::inflammation and vascular leakage}}.
cards.question: Meningococcal endotoxin can promote destructive {{c1::inflammation and vascular leakage}}.

cards.explanation: Its inflammatory disease involves interactions among the organism, LOS and host responses.
cards.text: The sexually transmitted infection caused by N. gonorrhoeae is {{c1::gonorrhoea}}.
cards.question: The sexually transmitted infection caused by N. gonorrhoeae is {{c1::gonorrhoea}}.

cards.explanation: Changes in expressed surface structures can aid immune evasion; this is not identical to a universal change in every molecule during every infection.
cards.text: Gonococcal LOS changes through {{c1::phase variation}}.
cards.question: Gonococcal LOS changes through {{c1::phase variation}}.

cards.explanation: The source lists pus and mucus with neutrophils. Pus itself already includes inflammatory cells, debris and fluid, rather than being an entirely separate cell-free substance.
cards.text: Gonococcal discharge is often rich in {{c1::neutrophils}}.
cards.question: Gonococcal discharge is often rich in {{c1::neutrophils}}.

cards.explanation: This relates to LPS/lipid A structural differences, not simply to the quantity of peptidoglycan.
cards.text: Chlamydial LPS is generally less immunostimulatory than typical {{c1::enterobacterial LPS}}.
cards.question: Chlamydial LPS is generally less immunostimulatory than typical {{c1::enterobacterial LPS}}.

cards.explanation: Lower relative immunostimulation is not the same as biological inactivity.
cards.text: Chlamydial LPS can still contribute to {{c1::innate inflammatory signalling}}.
cards.question: Chlamydial LPS can still contribute to {{c1::innate inflammatory signalling}}.

cards.explanation: The source links chronic tissue damage with infertility; the outcome is not inevitable and cannot be attributed only to LPS.
cards.text: A reproductive complication of persistent chlamydial infection is {{c1::scarring-associated infertility}}.
cards.question: A reproductive complication of persistent chlamydial infection is {{c1::scarring-associated infertility}}.

cards.explanation: Symptoms and tissue damage need not track together. The source’s peptidoglycan explanation is separate from the chemical structure of LPS.
cards.text: Asymptomatic chlamydial carriage can permit {{c1::unrecognised transmission}}.
cards.question: Asymptomatic chlamydial carriage can permit {{c1::unrecognised transmission}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts its typically painful ulcers with the classic painless primary syphilitic chancre; pain patterns alone are not diagnostic.
cards.text: Haemophilus ducreyi causes the genital ulcer disease {{c1::chancroid}}.
cards.question: Haemophilus ducreyi causes the genital ulcer disease {{c1::chancroid}}.

cards.explanation: This is an LOS example rather than a long-chain classical LPS molecule.
cards.text: H. ducreyi endotoxin lacks the long repeating {{c1::O-antigen chain}}.
cards.question: H. ducreyi endotoxin lacks the long repeating {{c1::O-antigen chain}}.

cards.explanation: The source links vascular injury and necrosis with inflammation. Other bacterial and host factors also contribute.
cards.text: LOS-driven cytokine release and neutrophil recruitment contribute to local {{c1::ulceration and tissue injury}}.
cards.question: LOS-driven cytokine release and neutrophil recruitment contribute to local {{c1::ulceration and tissue injury}}.

cards.explanation: This can involve contaminated food/water or exposure during sexual contact; it is not exclusively a foodborne pathway.
cards.text: Shigella is transmitted primarily by the {{c1::faecal–oral route}}.
cards.question: Shigella is transmitted primarily by the {{c1::faecal–oral route}}.

cards.explanation: This connects the variable polysaccharide structure with antigenic classification.
cards.text: Shigella serotypes are distinguished by the {{c1::O-antigen repeat region}} of LPS.
cards.question: Shigella serotypes are distinguished by the {{c1::O-antigen repeat region}} of LPS.

cards.explanation: The source emphasises this for Shigella; protection and cross-reactivity are more nuanced than one universal rule for all pathogens.
cards.text: O-antigen variation can make protective immune responses {{c1::serotype specific}}.
cards.question: O-antigen variation can make protective immune responses {{c1::serotype specific}}.

cards.explanation: These are examples, not the only routes.
cards.text: Campylobacter exposure is associated with undercooked poultry or {{c1::unpasteurised milk}}.
cards.question: Campylobacter exposure is associated with undercooked poultry or {{c1::unpasteurised milk}}.

cards.explanation: It lacks the long O-antigen chain described for standard LPS.
cards.text: C. jejuni endotoxin commonly has the truncated {{c1::LOS}} form.
cards.question: C. jejuni endotoxin commonly has the truncated {{c1::LOS}} form.

cards.explanation: The relevant ganglioside mimicry concerns the LOS oligosaccharide region, not simply the lipid A region. GM1/GD1a are source examples.
cards.text: Some C. jejuni LOS carbohydrate structures mimic human {{c1::nerve gangliosides}}.
cards.question: Some C. jejuni LOS carbohydrate structures mimic human {{c1::nerve gangliosides}}.

cards.explanation: This is a mechanism linking infection with an autoimmune complication, not direct bacterial invasion of every affected nerve.
cards.text: Antibodies that recognise bacterial LOS may cross-react with nerve tissue through {{c1::molecular mimicry}}.
cards.question: Antibodies that recognise bacterial LOS may cross-react with nerve tissue through {{c1::molecular mimicry}}.

cards.explanation: It occurs in a minority of infections. The slide’s separate epidural-abscess caption should not be treated as the definition or routine consequence of GBS.
cards.text: A recognised post-Campylobacter autoimmune complication is {{c1::Guillain–Barré syndrome}}.
cards.question: A recognised post-Campylobacter autoimmune complication is {{c1::Guillain–Barré syndrome}}.

cards.explanation: This describes the disease context and strain group, not every commensal intestinal E. coli.
cards.text: E. coli strains causing disease outside the gut are termed {{c1::extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC)}}.
cards.question: E. coli strains causing disease outside the gut are termed {{c1::extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC)}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from assuming every extraintestinal infection requires a newly acquired external organism.
cards.text: Movement of a host’s own organisms to another site can cause an {{c1::endogenous infection}}.
cards.question: Movement of a host’s own organisms to another site can cause an {{c1::endogenous infection}}.

cards.explanation: The source connects this with hypotension, DIC and organ injury; it does not mean every ExPEC infection causes a systemic cytokine storm.
cards.text: ExPEC lipid A signalling can activate NF-κB and excessive {{c1::cytokine release}}.
cards.question: ExPEC lipid A signalling can activate NF-κB and excessive {{c1::cytokine release}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses a necrotising-fasciitis case as an illustration. This is not the usual inevitable presentation of ExPEC disease.
cards.text: Microthrombi and inflammation can impair perfusion and cause tissue {{c1::hypoxia}}.
cards.question: Microthrombi and inflammation can impair perfusion and cause tissue {{c1::hypoxia}}.

cards.explanation: The source also lists cardiorespiratory and vascular effects. They overlap with other mediators rather than being unique signs of TNF action.
cards.text: TNF contributes to systemic inflammatory effects including {{c1::fever}}.
cards.question: TNF contributes to systemic inflammatory effects including {{c1::fever}}.

cards.explanation: The source calls these PMNs. This is a characteristic inflammatory pattern, not a diagnostic test of one cytokine.
cards.text: IL-1 is associated with fever, appetite loss and increased {{c1::polymorphonuclear leukocytes}}.
cards.question: IL-1 is associated with fever, appetite loss and increased {{c1::polymorphonuclear leukocytes}}.

cards.explanation: Recruitment and activation help contain infection but may also contribute to vascular injury.
cards.text: The chemokine especially linked with neutrophil chemotaxis in this lecture is {{c1::IL-8 (CXCL8)}}.
cards.question: The chemokine especially linked with neutrophil chemotaxis in this lecture is {{c1::IL-8 (CXCL8)}}.

cards.explanation: The source describes an amplifying mediator network, not a pathway in which every cytokine has only one source.
cards.text: TNF and IL-1 can promote secondary production of {{c1::IL-6}}.
cards.question: TNF and IL-1 can promote secondary production of {{c1::IL-6}}.

cards.explanation: Different prostanoids have different actions; do not assign every listed eicosanoid exactly the same effect.
cards.text: Prostaglandins can contribute to inflammatory {{c1::vasodilation}}.
cards.question: Prostaglandins can contribute to inflammatory {{c1::vasodilation}}.

cards.explanation: The source groups them broadly. LTB4 is strongly chemotactic, whereas cysteinyl leukotrienes have other vascular/airway effects; “all leukotrienes cause vasodilation” is too broad.
cards.text: Different leukotrienes can promote chemotaxis or increased {{c1::vascular permeability}}.
cards.question: Different leukotrienes can promote chemotaxis or increased {{c1::vascular permeability}}.

cards.explanation: Classical, lectin and alternative pathways feed into shared downstream functions.
cards.text: The three complement initiation routes converge on activation of {{c1::C3}}.
cards.question: The three complement initiation routes converge on activation of {{c1::C3}}.

cards.explanation: This is contrasted with lectin recognition and alternative activation on suitable surfaces.
cards.text: Antigen-bound antibody is the classic trigger shown for the {{c1::classical pathway}}.
cards.question: Antigen-bound antibody is the classic trigger shown for the {{c1::classical pathway}}.

cards.explanation: The source compares different initiation routes rather than three separate final outcomes.
cards.text: Recognition of microbial carbohydrates by mannose-binding lectin initiates the {{c1::lectin pathway}}.
cards.question: Recognition of microbial carbohydrates by mannose-binding lectin initiates the {{c1::lectin pathway}}.

cards.explanation: The same system can also contribute to host injury when excessive or dysregulated.
cards.text: Complement protects through inflammatory recruitment, opsonisation and {{c1::membrane damage}}.
cards.question: Complement protects through inflammatory recruitment, opsonisation and {{c1::membrane damage}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s LPS/properdin/factors description is a simplified surface-activation account, not one direct LPS receptor complex.
cards.text: The alternative pathway can amplify complement activation without requiring {{c1::antibody}}.
cards.question: The alternative pathway can amplify complement activation without requiring {{c1::antibody}}.

cards.explanation: Factor B/D interactions generate it on suitable surfaces; properdin stabilises it. This corrects reading the listed LPS-binding factors as a complete preformed complex.
cards.text: The alternative-pathway C3 convertase is {{c1::C3bBb}}.
cards.question: The alternative-pathway C3 convertase is {{c1::C3bBb}}.

cards.explanation: It supports the C3bBb complex rather than replacing the convertase’s catalytic components.
cards.text: The complement protein stabilising alternative C3 convertase is {{c1::properdin}}.
cards.question: The complement protein stabilising alternative C3 convertase is {{c1::properdin}}.

cards.explanation: The fragments have distinct roles; one is not simply an inactive version of the other.
cards.text: C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and {{c1::C3b}}.
cards.question: C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and {{c1::C3b}}.

cards.explanation: Coating a target makes it easier for complement-receptor-bearing phagocytes to bind and ingest it.
cards.text: Surface-bound C3b promotes phagocytic recognition through {{c1::opsonisation}}.
cards.question: Surface-bound C3b promotes phagocytic recognition through {{c1::opsonisation}}.

cards.explanation: C3a and C5a both have inflammatory/anaphylatoxin roles, but C3a is not an equivalent major neutrophil chemoattractant.
cards.text: The complement fragment most strongly associated here with neutrophil chemotaxis is {{c1::C5a}}.
cards.question: The complement fragment most strongly associated here with neutrophil chemotaxis is {{c1::C5a}}.

cards.explanation: C5b initiates the terminal membrane-attack assembly, whereas C5a is a soluble inflammatory mediator.
cards.text: C5 cleavage releases C5a and {{c1::C5b}}.
cards.question: C5 cleavage releases C5a and {{c1::C5b}}.

cards.explanation: This terminal complex can perforate susceptible target membranes.
cards.text: Assembly of C5b with C6–C9 produces the {{c1::membrane attack complex (MAC)}}.
cards.question: Assembly of C5b with C6–C9 produces the {{c1::membrane attack complex (MAC)}}.

cards.explanation: The periodontal diagram shows possible interactions with cytokines and bone-resorptive pathways; it does not establish that complement alone explains every lesion.
cards.text: Endotoxin-associated complement activation can amplify {{c1::local inflammation}}.
cards.question: Endotoxin-associated complement activation can amplify {{c1::local inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture places LPS above this model pathway. Sepsis-associated coagulation also prominently involves tissue-factor pathways and cannot be reduced to direct factor XII activation alone.
cards.text: The contact/intrinsic pathway factor named Hageman factor is {{c1::factor XII}}.
cards.question: The contact/intrinsic pathway factor named Hageman factor is {{c1::factor XII}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to the text: factor VIIIa is a cofactor of intrinsic tenase upstream, not part of a combined Xa–V–VIII prothrombinase. Calcium and phospholipid surfaces also support the complex.
cards.text: Activated factor X works with cofactor Va in the {{c1::prothrombinase complex}}.
cards.question: Activated factor X works with cofactor Va in the {{c1::prothrombinase complex}}.

cards.explanation: Thrombin is activated factor II (IIa) and acts on downstream substrates.
cards.text: Prothrombin is converted to {{c1::thrombin}}.
cards.question: Prothrombin is converted to {{c1::thrombin}}.

cards.explanation: This forms the structural clot network rather than converting fibrin back into fibrinogen.
cards.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into {{c1::fibrin}}.
cards.question: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into {{c1::fibrin}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram then enters a common pathway leading to thrombin and fibrin.
cards.text: The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at activation of {{c1::factor X}}.
cards.question: The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at activation of {{c1::factor X}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the factor-XII contact pathway and is important in infection-associated coagulation.
cards.text: The extrinsic pathway in the diagram begins with {{c1::tissue factor}} and factor VII/VIIa.
cards.question: The extrinsic pathway in the diagram begins with {{c1::tissue factor}} and factor VII/VIIa.

cards.explanation: The source diagram shows activation of XIII before stable clot formation.
cards.text: The factor cross-linking and stabilising fibrin is {{c1::factor XIIIa}}.
cards.question: The factor cross-linking and stabilising fibrin is {{c1::factor XIIIa}}.

cards.explanation: The clinical images on these pages are covered. The card tests the mechanism rather than guessing hidden signs.
cards.text: Widespread activation of clotting within the circulation is {{c1::disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)}}.
cards.question: Widespread activation of clotting within the circulation is {{c1::disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)}}.

cards.explanation: Ischaemia and hypoxia can contribute to organ injury even while inflammatory vascular leakage is also occurring.
cards.text: Microvascular fibrin thrombi can impair {{c1::tissue perfusion}}.
cards.question: Microvascular fibrin thrombi can impair {{c1::tissue perfusion}}.

cards.explanation: This explains the apparent paradox of clot formation with haemorrhage; the source provides no complete diagnostic thresholds or treatment protocol.
cards.text: DIC can cause bleeding as well as thrombosis because platelets and clotting factors are {{c1::consumed}}.
cards.question: DIC can cause bleeding as well as thrombosis because platelets and clotting factors are {{c1::consumed}}.

cards.explanation: LPS recognition drives inflammatory and vascular/coagulation cascades; the distinction from a single enzymatic protein exotoxin is important.
cards.text: Excessive endotoxin-associated damage is largely mediated by the {{c1::host response}}.
cards.question: Excessive endotoxin-associated damage is largely mediated by the {{c1::host response}}.

cards.explanation: Serotype-specific responses may not cover every variant. The source does not imply vaccines against all Gram-negative infections are impossible.
cards.text: Variation in surface polysaccharides can complicate {{c1::vaccine coverage}}.
cards.question: Variation in surface polysaccharides can complicate {{c1::vaccine coverage}}.

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 2
slides.text:
Learning outcomes
•
Describe the structure of the bacterial endotoxin
•
Understand how the endotoxin is produced, and the
effects that the endotoxin has on patients

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 3
slides.text:
Definition
•
Endotoxins are toxic molecules associated with the outer membrane
and cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria
-
Lipopolysaccharides of Gram-negative bacteria (‘true’ endotoxins)
-
Lipoteichoic acids of Gram-positive bacteria (‘endotoxin-like’)
-
Muramyl peptides of Gram-positive bacteria (‘endotoxin-like’)
•
Small amounts are produced by viable / intact cells
•
Large amounts are released on disintegration of the cell due to:
- Bacterial cell membrane attacked by complement complex
- Bacterial cells killed intracellularly by phagocytosis
- Bacterial cells killed by antibiotics targeting the cell-wall

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 4
slides.text:
Disturbance of physiological cascades by 
endotoxin

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 5
slides.text:
Lipopolysaccharide (Gram-negative)
•
The major endotoxin molecule in bacteria
•
Found in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, 
but only becomes ‘active’ in its cell-free form
•
Heat stable
•
Has three components:
- Lipid A is common to most Gram-negatives and is the most toxic part of the molecule
- The core polysaccharide is genus-specific, and contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-C sugars
- O-specific polysaccharide is variable in structure and may account for variable toxicity

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 6
slides.text: Generic structure of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 7
slides.text:
Variations in lipopolysaccharide structure
• Bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae and 
Pseudomonadaceae have the ‘standard’ LPS
• Polysaccharide consists of about 20 – 40 repeated 
oligosaccharide subunits
• Neisseria, Haemophilus, Bordetella, and Bacteroides 
have no O-specific 
polysaccharide side-chain – therefore their ‘LPS’ is 
truncated, and known as a ‘lipooligosaccharide’ 
(LOS)
• Chlamydia has only the lipid A + ketodeoxyoctonate 
(various 7-carbons)
Arenas (2012) Endocrine, Metabolic, and Immune Disorders

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 8
slides.text:
Toxicity of lipopolysaccharides
•
‘Lipid A’ is the most toxic component
•
The polysaccharide component 
probably affects activity 
by increasing solubility
•
It also controls micelle size in free 
molecules, the smaller the 
micelle size the more active the 
molecule

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 9
slides.text:
Action of lipopolysaccharides
•
The LPS molecule binds to an LPS-
binding protein (LBP) in blood
•
The complex binds to CD14 receptors 
on macrophages and on endothelial 
cells, which is then presented to TLR4 
receptors…
•
Macrophages release a variety of 
molecular mediators which affect:
- The immune system
- The complement cascade
- The coagulation cascade

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 10
slides.text:
Effects of Lipopolysaccharide
•
Consequences of small amounts of LPS – protective
- Moderate fever
- Stimulation of the immune system
- Bacterial death
•
Consequences of large amounts of LPS – sepsis
- High fever
- Low blood pressure
- Increased respiratory and heart rate
- Lung and kidney failure
- Dissemination intravascular coagulation (DIC)
- Systemic inflammatory response

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 11
slides.text:
Neisseria meningitidis
• N. meningitidis (Gram-negative)
colonises the nasopharynx
• Bacteria then invade through the
epithelium directly into the bloodstream
• The bacteria cross the blood-brain
barrier (BBB) to reach the meninges
and cerebrospinal fluid…
• The bacterial endotoxin increases
vascular permeability, which allowed 
the crossing of the BBB and 
subsequent destructive inflammation →
Musubire et al., (2013) – meningococcal
 disease autopsy. J AIDS Clin Res.

slides.text:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
• N. gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmissible 
Gram-negative bacteria which causes 
gonorrhoea
• Its endotoxin’s interactions with the immune 
system are the major causative agent of 
disease symptoms
• The LOS structure is able to
change through phase variation – 
resulting in immune evasion
• Gonorrhoea discharge is composed of 
pus, mucus, and neutrophils.

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 13
slides.text:
Chlamydia trachomatis
Chlamydia proctitis Arevalo et al., 
(2022) BMC Gastroenterology
• C. trachomatis is a Gram-negative bacterium that causes
the sexually transmissible infection: chlamydia
• C. trachomatis has an unusual LPS, as it lacks (or has 
comparatively very small amounts) of peptidoglycan 
• So while the LPS is present, it is less immunogenic 
in comparison to the ‘traditional’ LPS found in enteric pathogens
• However… it still contributes to the development of 
initial inflammatory signals, activation of innate immunity,
and damage to epithelial cells
• The ‘slower’ and relatively unnoticed damage caused by 
chlamydia leads to infertility and chronic scarring, and also 
facilitates asymptomatic carriage and transmission to others

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 14
slides.text:
Haemophilus ducreyi
•
H. ducreyi causes chancroid – a genital ulcer disease
•
These ulcers are painful (unlike syphilis)
•
As with Neisseria spp., its endotoxin ‘LPS’ lacks 
the O-antigen repeating units
•
The LOS contributes to local tissue damage and 
ulcer formation due to vascular damage and necrosis
through recruitment of neutrophils and cytokine release
(TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8)
•
The endotoxin is the primary driver of the acute 
inflammatory response
Chancroid ulcers of the penis
Lewis (2015) Clinics in Dermatology

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 15
slides.text:
Shigella spp.
Anderson et al., (2016) Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
•
Shigella species are Gram negative 
bacteria that are transmitted
via the faecal-oral route (sexually or
by consuming faecally contaminated food/water)
•
There are four species of Shigella:
 
- S. sonnei 
 
- S. flexneri 
 
- S. boydii
 
- S. dysenteriae
•
Shigella spp. can be further defined into
serotypes, which are determined by the
O-antigen repeat region of the LPS…
Immunity is serotype specific

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 16
slides.text:
Campylobacter spp.
Campylobacter spp. colitis: Kwok et al., (2016) 
International Journals of Surgery Case Reports  
Epidural abscess caused by Campylobacter spp.
-associated Guillain–Barré syndrome 
• Campylobacter spp. are Gram-negative
bacteria, associated with the consumption
of undercooked poultry or unpasteurised milk
• C. jejuni lacks the O-antigen region of its 
endotoxin, and has a hypervariable Lipid-A
region
• The endotoxin structures of C. jejuni mimic
human nerve gangliosides (such as GM1, GD1a)
• This causes the production of auto-antibodies,
which cross-react with nerve tissue and cause
Guillain-Barré Syndrome (a neurological disorder)

colitis, behind this box

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 17
slides.text:
Extraintestinal Pathogenic Escherichia coli 
(ExPEC)
•
Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) are 
strains of E. coli that cause disease outside of the 
intestinal tract
•
Typically, they cause disease because of 
endogenous infection (from within the host’s 
body, moving from one site to another)
•
The recognition of Lipid A by the TLR4 activates 
the NF-kB pathway, leading to the excessive 
release of cytokines (TNF, IL1, IL6, etc.) in a 
‘cytokine storm’, complement, and coagulation
•
Fever, hypotension, DIC, and endotoxic shock
may occur as a result. Ischemia + inflammation + tissue hypoxia, microthrombi 
→ necrosis of the tissue  → necrotising fasciitis 
Necrotising fasciitis mediated by ExPEC (E. coli)
Abdallah et al., (2023) Ear, Nose and Throat Journal

Mechanisms of Action
Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
- Produced secondary to TNF and IL-1
- Sustains prostaglandin and leukotriene production 
Interleukin-8 (IL-8)
- Produced secondary to TNF and IL-1
- Induces prostaglandin and leukotriene production
- Neutrophil chemotaxis
- Contributes to vascular damage
Prostaglandin: Vasodilation
Increased vascular permeability
- Leukotriene: Vasodilation, vascular
permeability, phagocyte chemotaxis

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 22
slides.text:
Activation of the Complement ‘Alternative 
Pathway’ 
LPS binds to properdin and factors B, D, 
and Mg2+
-
Forms C3 convertase 
-
C3 convertase acts on C3
- Converts C3 into C3a and C3b
-
C3b binds to the bacterial surface
- promotes the conversion of C5 into C5a 
and C5b
-
Effects of C3a and C5a
- Chemotaxis, inflammation, 
vasomotor effects
-
C3b on bacteria promotes binding to 
phagocytes - Opsonisation
-
Addition of C5b, C6, C7, C8, C9
- Forms membrane attack complex

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 24
slides.text:
Activation of the Coagulation Intrinsic Pathway
• LPS activates Factor XII (Hageman Factor)
- Activates a cascade resulting in activated
Factor X
• Factor X combines with Factor V and VIII to form
thrombokinase (thromboplastin)
- Converts prothrombin → thrombin
• Thrombin acts on fibrinogen
- Converts fibrinogen → soluble fibrin → stable fibrin
• Coagulation in the capillaries… disseminated intravascular coagulation

slides.topic: Endotoxins — LPS, Immune Activation & Coagulation — page 28
slides.text:
Summary
• Endotoxins are a significant causative agent of
disease by Gram-negative bacteria
• Endotoxins are potent immune-activators, where large amounts
of endotoxins being present lead to a pathological ‘overreaction’
by the immune system
• Hypervariability within the LPS structure can lead 
to immune evasion, and serotype-specific 
immunity for some pathogens… making vaccine
development difficult too
